articles.title: Padre Marcelo Rossi fala sobre significado de 31 anos de sacerdócio  | G1
articles.standfirst: Sacerdote usou o significado do "Jubileu de Nácar" para falar sobre a cura de dores físicas e emocionais neste domingo (6) em Franca (SP). Religioso refletiu sobre trajetória na mídia e sobre esgotamento emocional que atinge os jovens.
articles.summary: No Hallel em Franca, Padre Marcelo Rossi celebrou seu Jubileu de Nácar e refletiu sobre a importância da fé para superar o burnout e a depressão na juventude.
articles.body:
Durante sua participação no Hallel, em Franca (SP), neste domingo (6), o padre Marcelo Rossi falou sobre seus 31 anos de ordenação que está completando em 2026.

Ele aproveitou o significado da data, o Jubileu de Nácar, para refletir sobre sua missão como sacerdote e deixar uma mensagem sobre a importância da fé para a superação das dores.

"Nácar é a substância que a ostra produz quando ela é ferida. A ostra ferida produz a pérola preciosa. Então, neste ano, Deus tem usado profundamente, vai me usar aqui, para levar, tocar as feridas das pessoas e levá-las pelo sangue de Jesus, que é mais do que o nácar, a transformação de pessoas", disse.

🔎 Celebrado ao se atingir 31 anos de uma união ou consagração, o termo "Jubileu de Nácar" faz referência à madrepérola, que reveste o interior das conchas de moluscos. O nácar é liberado pela ostra para isolar corpos estranhos e curar ferimentos em seu tecido interno.

A celebração ocorre em uma fase emblemática para o padre, com 59 anos. Ao longo de sua caminhada, padre Marcelo Rossi se consolidou como um dos maiores expoentes da música católica no Brasil.

Padre Marcelo Rossi, no Hallel 2026, em Franca (SP). — Foto: g1 Ribeirão Preto e Franca

Sua atuação alcançou enorme repercussão na grande mídia e nos meios não católicos, registrando recordes de vendas na indústria fonográfica e liderança de audiência em transmissões de rádio e TV.

"Hoje nós vemos todos que estão surgindo, pessoas que estão aparecendo e levando as pessoas a amar Jesus, isso não tem preço. Quando você se apaixona por Jesus você quer levar esse amor a outras pessoas."

Aproveitando a passagem pelo interior de São Paulo, o sacerdote também propôs uma reflexão sobre a saúde mental e a espiritualidade, temas frequentes em suas pregações e livros.

Para o padre, as pressões cotidianas têm gerado uma sobrecarga precoce nas novas gerações, tornando indispensável o acolhimento religioso. O padre advertiu sobre o cansaço percebido na juventude que busca amparo na fé.

"Hoje os nossos jovens estão velhos (...) Eles estão passando por tantas experiências ruins que estão agora na busca de Deus. É a hora de levar esse Deus maravilhoso. Os jovens de hoje queimaram etapas. Eles estão tendo experiência de burnout , de depressão e nós temos que levar a esperança que é Jesus", afirmou.

Considerado um dos maiores festivais de evangelização da América Latina, o Hallel 2026 acontece no Parque de Exposições Fernando Costa, em Franca até segunda-feira (7), com entrada gratuita.

Sob o tema “Eu sou o Caminho, a Verdade e a Vida”, a 39ª edição reúne cerca de 80 atrações entre pregações, missas e apresentações musicais.

No palco central, os shows foram abertos na sexta-feira (4) por Juninho Cassimiro e a banda Rosa de Saron. O sábado (5) foi marcado pela participação de Flávio Vítor, a estreia das irmãs Maria Raquel e Maria Joana, do Instituto Hesed, além do show de retorno do padre Fábio de Melo.

Neste domingo (6), além da missa celebrada pelo padre Marcelo Rossi, o público acompanhou as apresentações de Gerados pela Imaculada, Anjos de Resgate e Comunidade Colo de Deus.

O encerramento do evento ocorre na segunda-feira (7) com apresentações do padre Adriano Zandoná e da Fraternidade São João Paulo II.

articles.title: Expointer tem faturamento de R$ 6,18 bi e recorde de público em um dia | G1
articles.standfirst: Este domingo (6) marcou o último dia da 49ª Expointer, que registrou dois recordes e divulgou os números das vendas neste final de semana.
articles.summary: Este domingo (6) marcou o último dia da 49ª Expointer, que registrou dois recordes e divulgou os números das vendas neste final de semana.
articles.body:
Expointer — Foto: Jefferson Botega/ Agencia RBS

Este domingo (6) marcou o último dia da 49ª Expointer, uma das maiores feiras agropecuárias da América Latina , que ocorre anualmente em Esteio, na Região Metropolitana de Porto Alegre. Em 2026, o evento teve alta no faturamento e bateu dois recordes.

A feira teve faturamento de R$ 6,18 bilhões neste ano, segundo balanço divulgado na tarde deste domingo (9). O valor representa uma alta de 40% em relação ao comercializado em 2025 , quando as vendas totais foram de R$ 4,42 bilhões, mas ainda fica aquém dos anos de 2024 (R$ 8,1 bilhões), 2023 (R$ 7,98 bilhões) e 2022 (R$ 7,14 bilhões).

Os principais números foram em vendas de máquinas e implementos agrícolas (R$ 5,46 bilhões), comercialização de animais (R$ 21,98 milhões), comércio e alimentação (R$ 17 milhões), agroindústria familiar (R$ 14,4 milhões) e artesanato (R$ 2,1 milhões).

Ao menos dois recordes foram batidos na Expointer 2026. O Pavilhão da Agricultura Familiar comercializou R$ 2.644.756,21 somente no sábado (5). Essa foi a maior cifra da história para um único dia . O recorde anterior era de R$ 2.254.759,13 em 2025, também no segundo sábado da feira.

Também no sábado foi registrado o maior público da história da Expointer para um único dia : 155.825 pessoas . O recorde anterior havia sido alcançado no segundo domingo de 2025: 147.812 pessoas.

articles.title: Confira o dia dos candidatos ao Governo do Piauí neste domingo (6) | G1

articles.title: Veja a agenda dos candidatos ao governo do Ceará neste domingo | G1
articles.standfirst: Quatro candidatos tiveram agendas públicas: Ciro Gomes (PSDB); Delegado Huggo (Missão); Elmano de Freitas (PT) e Vera Lúcia (Novo).
articles.summary: Quatro candidatos tiveram agendas públicas: Ciro Gomes (PSDB); Delegado Huggo (Missão); Elmano de Freitas (PT) e Vera Lúcia (Novo).
articles.body:
Candidatos a governador do Ceará em 2026 — Foto: Fabiane de Paula/SVM; Thiago Gadelha/SVM; Kid Junior/SVM; Divulgação

Os candidatos ao governo do Ceará apostam em carreatas e motocarreata durante agenda de campanha eleitoral neste domingo (6). Eles se dividiram entre a região metropolitana de Fortaleza e o interior do estado.

Quatro candidatos tiveram agendas públicas: Ciro Gomes (PSDB); Delegado Huggo (Missão); Elmano de Freitas (PT) e Vera Lúcia (Novo).

Danilo Soares (Democrata), Ieri Braga (PCO) e Zé Batista (PSTU) não divulgaram agenda pública para este dia.

A equipe de Serley Leal (UP) comunicou que o candidato precisou cancelar a agenda prevista para este final de semana por motivo de saúde.

Ciro Gomes, candidato do PSDB, participou de carreata, no fim da tarde deste domingo, em Acaraú, no interior do estado. Ele esteve acompanhado do candidato a vice, Roberto Claudio (União), e do candidato ao Senado, Alcides Fernandes (PL), entre outras lideranças.

Delegado Huggo, candidato do Missão, participou de carreata em Fortaleza ao lado do presidenciável Renan Santos, do mesmo partido. A carreata começou na Igreja Nossa Senhora da Saúde, no bairro Mucuripe, e foi até o bairro Vicente Pinzon.

Elmano de Freitas, candidato do PT à reeleição, participou de caminhada em Beberibe, na região metropolitana de Fortaleza, na manhã deste domingo. À tarde, Elmano foi a Forquilha, na região norte do estado, para realizar uma motocarreata. O candidato do PT encerrou a agenda deste domingo em um evento de campanha em São Benedito, no Vale do Jaguaribe, à noite.

Vera Lúcia, candidata do Novo, realizou carreata no bairro Granja Portugal, em Fortaleza, na noite deste domingo.

articles.title: Fibromialgia: as pessoas que vivem com dores inexplicáveis e ainda lidam com a incompreensão dos outros | G1
articles.standfirst: Neste episódio do podcast “Isso é Fantástico”, você ouve as entrevistas do repórter Pedro Vedova com o presidente da Sociedade Brasileira de Reumatologia, José Eduardo Martinez, e com a psicóloga clínica Reny Oliveira.
articles.summary: Neste episódio do podcast “Isso é Fantástico”, você ouve as entrevistas do repórter Pedro Vedova com o presidente da Sociedade Brasileira de Reumatologia, José Eduardo Martinez, e com a psicóloga clínica Reny Oliveira.
articles.body:
Uma dor que pode transformar um show, um sorriso ou até lavar a louça em um desafio. A fibromialgia atinge cerca de 6 milhões de brasileiros , segundo a Sociedade Brasileira de Reumatologia . e, para quem tem a síndrome, a dor é só uma parte do problema. Cansaço, alterações no sono e dificuldades para manter a rotina também podem fazer parte do dia a dia.

Agora uma nova lei federal ampliou a proteção a essas pessoas. Mas o que a ciência já consegue explicar sobre essa dor? Por que ela acontece? E como tratar uma doença que, muitas vezes, é invisível aos olhos de quem está de fora?

Neste episódio do podcast “Isso é Fantástico” , você ouve as entrevistas do repórter Pedro Vedova com o presidente da Sociedade Brasileira de Reumatologia, José Eduardo Martinez, e com a psicóloga clínica Reny Oliveira.

articles.title: Veja como foi a agenda de campanha dos candidatos ao governo do Pará | G1
articles.standfirst: Confira as atividades de campanha de Araceli Lemos; Daniel Santos; Gal Leite; Hana Ghassan; Ruth Reis e Well Macêdo.
articles.summary: Confira as atividades de campanha de Araceli Lemos; Daniel Santos; Gal Leite; Hana Ghassan; Ruth Reis e Well Macêdo.
articles.body:
Candidatos ao Governo do Pará nas Eleições 2026 — Foto: Reprodução

Os candidatos ao governo do Pará cumpriram compromissos de campanha neste sábado (5) e domingo (6) de setembro.

Entre as atividades do fim de semana, os candidatos ao cargo realizaram caminhadas em feiras, carreatas, visitas a apoiadores no comércio, inaugurações de espaços de campanha, panfletagens, encontros políticos, reuniões virtuais e mobilizações de rua.

Os eventos foram realizados em Belém e também em cidades do interior do estado.

O primeiro turno das eleições está marcado para o dia 4 de outubro de 2026. O segundo turno, caso seja necessário, ocorrerá no dia 25 do mesmo mês.

Veja, abaixo, como foi o dia de campanha de cada candidato, em ordem alfabética:

No sábado (5), a candidata realizou, pela manhã uma caminhada na feira municipal de Benevides e, participou da inauguração de um espaço de campanha no município. À noite, Araceli esteve em Belém para a inauguração do comitê de um candidato a deputado estadual.

No domingo (6), a candidata visitou a feira do Conjunto Cordeiro de Farias, no bairro do Tapanã, em Belém, durante a manhã, e encerrou o dia com uma caminhada na orla de Santarém , no oeste do estado, à noite.

No sábado (5), o candidato Daniel Santos cumpriu agenda no sudeste do estado, com compromissos nos municípios de Xinguara , pela manhã. Pela tarde, o candidato esteve em Redenção , no sudeste paraense.

No domingo (6), o candidato do PODEMOS realizou, pela manhã, uma atividade de mobilização de rua, com concentração na Avenida Bernardo Sayão, entre a Rua dos Caripunas e a Rua dos Timbiras, em Belém.

Até a publicação desta reportagem, a candidata não enviou a agenda de compromissos realizados no fim de semana.

No sábado (5), pela manhã, a candidata realizou uma carreata em Castanhal . À tarde, participou de outra carreata em Abaetetuba e esteve em Ananindeua para o lançamento da campanha de um candidato a deputado estadual. À noite, ela participou de uma nova carreata em Benevides.

No domingo (6), Hana Ghassan realizou, pela manhã, uma carreata em Belém, com concentração no Portal da Amazônia, no bairro do Jurunas.

No sábado (5), durante a amanhã a candidata realizou visitas a apoiadores no comércio de Belém . À tarde e à noite, Ruth Reis cumpriu compromissos de agenda no ITQ.

No domingo (6), a candidata não teve compromissos de campanha divulgados por sua assessoria.

No sábado (5), a candidata participou, pela manhã, do ato "Grito dos Excluídos" no bairro da Terra Firme, em Belém. À tarde, Well Macêdo integrou uma roda de conversa on-line sobre a luta internacional das mulheres entre Brasil e Angola e, no início da noite, realizou panfletagem em frente ao Hangar.

No domingo (6), a candidata fez uma caminhada com panfletagem na feira de Marituba , na Região Metropolitana de Belém, pela manhã, e participou de uma reunião on-line com o movimento negro à tarde.

articles.title: Acidente em Paulínia: caminhão destrói muro de casa e fere motorista | G1
articles.standfirst: Três veículos também foram atingidos pelo caminhão - dois estacionados na rua e um que estava dentro do imóvel. Acidente ocorreu entre Cosmópolis e Paulínia
articles.summary: Caminhão bate em casa em Paulínia, atinge caminhonete estacionada e deixa motorista ferido; Defesa Civil avaliou danos no imóvel neste domingo.
articles.body:
O motorista de um caminhão ficou ferido após o veículo bater no muro de uma casa na tarde deste domingo (6), entre Cosmópolis (SP) e Paulínia (SP). Três veículos também foram atingidos - dois estacionados na rua e um que estava dentro do imóvel.

O acidente ocorreu na Avenida Severino Beraldo, que fica no limite dos municípios. Segundo a Guarda Municipal de Cosmópolis, houve briga com agressão entre a família do caminhoneiro e moradores do bairro.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, o motorista foi socorrido por uma ambulância do município. Até última atualização desta reportagem, não havia informações sobre o estado de saúde dele.

A Defesa Civil foi acionada por volta das 16h15 e, segundo a prefeitura, apesar dos danos na casa, não houve necessidade de interdição. Duas viaturas estiverem no local para prestar apoio.

Caminhão destrói muro de casa; motorista ficou ferido — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

articles.title: Maroon 5 no Brasil: banda abre turnê com show no interior de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Adam Levine e banda subiram ao palco em São José do Rio Preto (SP) para a primeira apresentação do grupo em uma cidade do interior, abrindo a turnê brasileira de "Love is Like".
articles.summary: Maroon 5 iniciou a turnê Love Is Like em São José do Rio Preto, na primeira apresentação da banda no interior brasileiro antes do Rock in Rio.
articles.body:
A banda Maroon 5 durante apresentação em São José do Rio Preto (SP), na noite deste domingo (6), na abertura da turnê brasileira de "Love is Like" — Foto: Henrique Souza/g1

O Maroon 5 subiu ao palco às 20h35 deste domingo (6) para o show inédito em São José do Rio Preto (SP), diante de um público estimado pelos organizadores em 25 mil pessoas, no Recinto de Exposições Alberto Bertelli Lucatto, depois de uma tarde de chuva, filas e muita expectativa . E a banda já começou colocando os fãs para cantar com Harder to Breathe , um dos primeiros sucessos da carreira.

A apresentação marca a primeira vez que o Maroon 5 faz um show em uma cidade do interior do Brasil e também a estreia da turnê Love Is Like no país. A banda será um dos destaques do Rock In Rio (leia mais abaixo) .

Antes do Maroon 5 aparecer no palco, o Lagum teve a missão de preparar o público para uma das apresentações mais aguardadas do ano em Rio Preto.

A banda mineira ficou cerca de 30 minutos no palco. Mesmo com a expectativa concentrada no Maroon 5, o público respondeu bem à apresentação e manteve o clima de festa no recinto.

A banda Lagum durante a abertura do show do Maroon 5, no recinto de exposições de São José do Rio Preto (SP), na noite deste domingo (6) — Foto: Henrique Souza/g1

Após o show em Rio Preto, primeira parada da banda no Brasil, o Maroon 5 segue para São Paulo , onde toca nesta terça-feira (8). Depois, tem Salvador (quinta, dia 10), e Rio de Janeiro , onde será atração do ck in Rio , no sábado (dia 12).

A apresentação em Rio Preto também coloca a cidade, que vem se destacando como rota de shows internacionais, como a primeira e única do interior do Brasil a receber a banda nesta passagem pelo país.

articles.title: Hurricane Marie sparks mass flooding in Seal Beach in California on Labor Day weekend
articles.summary: Powerful swells from Hurricane Marie are flooding beaches, trapping vehicles and prompting water rescues along the Southern California coast as dangerous rip...
articles.body:
Hurricane Marie is causing flooding, water rescues, and dangerous rip currents along the Southern California coastline from Los Angeles County to Orange County.

Despite not making landfall in California, the storm is already impacting beaches with ocean water surging into parking lots near the Seal Beach Pier and flooding low-lying areas.

The National Weather Service has issued warnings for coastal flooding, dangerous rip currents, beach erosion, and large waves across Southern California as a result of Hurricane Marie's effects.

Hurricane Marie is impacting the Southern California coastline with powerful swells and dangerous rip currents triggering flooding, water rescues, and a frantic effort to keep ocean water away from homes.

The storm, churning in the eastern Pacific off the coast of Baja California, is not expected to make landfall in the Golden State — but it is already hitting beaches spanning Los Angeles County to Orange County.

At Seal Beach on Saturday, ocean water surged into parking lots near the pier, flooding low-lying areas and trapping vehicles.

Video obtained by ABC7 showed roughly a dozen people joining forces to push one overwhelmed vehicle out of the floodwaters.

By nighttime, wet sand had spread across the boardwalk and flooding was still visible at homes along the shoreline.

"This is crazy. I've lived here for 20+ years, and usually we get like 1- to 2-foot waves. But when we get the storm to come in here, it's like, crazy. We're just not used to that," Seal Beach resident Clifford Scarborough said.

Crews responded by constructing a berm and pumping seawater back toward the ocean. The 8th Street and 10th Street parking lots that were inundated are expected to remain closed through Wednesday.

The dangerous conditions weren't limited to Seal Beach.

In Manhattan Beach , a lifeguard rescue was caught on video as towering swells and powerful currents created hazardous conditions, despite Marie remaining hundreds of miles away.

"It's extremely concerning — having children, you're always on high alert," Melissa Sann of Mid-Wilshire said.

Los Angeles County lifeguards are preparing for a particularly busy holiday weekend, with officials anticipating more than 1,000 water rescues. On a typical day, that number can be around 500.

"We're expecting to see these elevated wave heights in the 3- to 5-foot range, with sets up to 6- to 8-feet up in some of our standout beaches up in Zuma Beach and Malibu," Los Angeles County Fire Department ocean lifeguard specialist Jake Miller told ABC7.

Lifeguards are warning beachgoers to check conditions before entering the water and to recognize their own limits as the storm-generated swells continue to arrive.

The National Weather Service has warned that Marie's effects could include coastal flooding, dangerous rip currents, beach erosion and large waves across Southern California.

"There is an increased risk for ocean drowning," the NWS warned, saying rip currents could become "widespread and very strong" and potentially pull swimmers and surfers away from shore.

The agency also warned that large breaking waves could injure people , sweep beachgoers from rocks and beaches, and overturn small boats near shore.

Low-lying coastal areas could see seawater flooding around high tide, particularly vulnerable stretches including Avalon, Long Beach's Alamitos Peninsula and the coastline from Oxnard to Malibu, including Point Mugu, according to the NWS.

The weather service has issued coastal flood, high surf and small craft advisories, along with a beach hazards statement, for parts of Southern California through Tuesday.

Meanwhile, the National Hurricane Center said Marie is expected to weaken steadily and become a post-tropical remnant low by Wednesday.

But the storm's swells are expected to continue affecting Southern California for several days, potentially creating life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions.

Back in Seal Beach, Scarborough said the weekend's flooding was a stark reminder of the ocean's power. "It just shows you how powerful it is. We have to respect nature," he said.

outhern California is getting an unusually wet taste of September as moisture associated with Hurricane Marie spreads across the region, with rain falling across Los Angeles and Ventura counties Sunday.

Downtown Los Angeles has recorded more than half an inch of rain, adding to a weekend weather pattern that is highly unusual for a region where most annual rainfall typically arrives during the cooler months. The National Weather Service said rainfall totals across Los Angeles County were generally between 0.10 and 0.33 inches Sunday morning, with some locations topping 0.50 inches.

As Marie's moisture pulls away, Southern California is expected to quickly transition from rain and cooler temperatures to a significant warming trend. The National Weather Service is forecasting warmer and drier conditions beginning Monday, with temperatures running above normal by midweek.

That means residents could go from a wet Labor Day weekend to a potentially intense heat spell within days, with the warmest conditions expected across inland areas.

articles.title: What's in a name? Population Authority shares most popular baby names ahead of Rosh Hashanah
articles.summary: Mohammed, Ariel, and Avigail topped Israel’s lists, with a total of 179,398 babies registered in Israel’s Population Registry as of Sunday morning, September...
articles.body:
Mohammed, Ariel, and Avigail were the most popular names given to babies in Israel during the Hebrew year 5786, with Mohammed being the most common name among boys across the general population.

Avigail was the most popular girls' name in Israel in 5786, followed by Miriam and Lia, with Avigail also topping the rankings among Jewish girls.

Jerusalem had the highest number of registered births in Israel during 5786, with 23,336 babies, followed by Bnei Brak and Tel Aviv-Jaffa.

Mohammed, Ariel, and Avigail topped Israel's lists, with a total of 179,398 babies registered in Israel's Population Registry as of Sunday morning, September 6.

Mohammed, Ariel, and Avigail topped Israel's lists of the most popular names given to babies during the Hebrew year 5786, according to Population and Immigration Authority data released on Sunday ahead of Rosh Hashanah .

A total of 179,398 babies had been registered in Israel's Population Registry as of Sunday morning, September 6, the authority said.

Mohammed was the most common name among boys across Israel's general population, followed by Ariel, Yosef, Adam, David, Omer, Rafael, Lavi, Michael, and Eitan.

Among Jewish boys, Ariel took first place. David ranked second, followed by Rafael, Lavi, Uri, Michael, Eliya, Eitan, Yehuda, and Ari.

Ariel's position at the top continues its strong showing in recent years. In 2024, it was also the most popular name among Jewish boys according to Population and Immigration Authority figures, while David ranked second and Lavi third. Earlier baby-name data showed Ariel leading Jewish boys in 2024.

Avigail was the most popular girls' name both across the general population and among Jewish Israelis in 5786.

In the overall ranking for girls, Avigail was followed by Miriam, Lia, Libi, Tamar, Yael, Ayala, Sarah, Ella, and Naya.

Among Jewish girls, Libi came in second after Avigail, followed by Tamar, Yael, Lia, Ella, Ayala, Sarah, Noa, and Naya.

Avigail has maintained an unusually strong run at the top of the rankings. Population and Immigration Authority figures for 2024 also placed the name first among Jewish girls, marking its second consecutive year in the top spot at the time. Avigail also topped Israel's 2024 rankings

More recent Central Bureau of Statistics data covering children born in 2024 similarly found Avigail to be the most popular name among Jewish girls, while traditional and biblical names continued to dominate many of the rankings. That analysis placed David first among Jewish boys in its separate dataset, followed by Levi and Ariel. Israeli parents continued to favor traditional names in CBS data

Mohammed's place at the top of the overall boys' ranking also continues a long-running pattern. The name topped the nationwide boys' list in data released ahead of Rosh Hashanah in 2022 as well, when Adam and Yosef followed it. Mohammed has led nationwide baby-name rankings in previous years

Jerusalem recorded by far the largest number of registered births during 5786, with 23,336 babies.

Bnei Brak ranked second with 8,225 births, while Tel Aviv-Jaffa was third with 7,405.

Beit Shemesh followed with 6,974 births, ahead of Ashdod with 4,031 and Haifa with 3,421.

Rishon LeZion registered 3,413 births, Netanya 3,343, Petah Tikva 3,338, and Modi'in Illit 3,113.

The figures were released as Israel prepared to enter the Hebrew year 5787, with Rosh Hashanah beginning on Friday evening.

articles.title: Built in 1928, this New Zealand swing bridge was nearly demolished; locals fought to save it and are now restoring it
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For years, the old Kopu Bridge was a familiar landmark for travellers heading into the Coromandel, but it was perhaps best known for the traffic queue.
articles.body: For years, the old Kopu Bridge was a familiar landmark for travellers heading into the Coromandel, but it was perhaps best known for the traffic queues that built up as vehicles waited to cross the Waihou River. The narrow bridge could carry traffic in only one direction at a time, turning busy journeys into slow ones. Its role changed in December 2011, when a new two-lane bridge opened nearby, as reported by NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi. The old structure was closed, and demolition was considered as its future remained uncertain. A community campaign, however, argued that the historic bridge was worth saving. After more than six years of negotiations, the Kopu Bridge and Community Trust took over the structure from the New Zealand Transport Agency in March 2018. Rather than disappear, the bridge entered a new chapter. The Trust began restoring it for pedestrians and cyclists, creating a link alongside the Hauraki Rail Trail and preserving a familiar piece of the region’s transport history.How the historic Kopu Bridge became New Zealand’s unique swing-span bridgeThe Kopu Bridge was built in difficult conditions and opened in 1928. The Waihou River had a soft and muddy bottom, which made construction challenging. Engineers divided the bridge into more than 20 spans and drove piles as deep as 70 feet into the riverbed to support the piers. The lower sections were made from timber because concrete piles could not withstand the pounding at that depth. The bridge also had to allow steamers to pass along the river. At the centre, a swing span could open to create a 50-foot passage for vessels. This feature became an important part of the bridge’s design. The bridge was built when river transport played an important role in the Hauraki Plains and helped connect the developing farming area with the wider region.How the local community fought to save the historic Kopu BridgeThe bridge’s future became uncertain after the new two-lane crossing opened in 2011. With traffic moved to the new structure, the old bridge was closed, and its future came under scrutiny. The Kopu Bridge and Community Trust, however, argued that the historic crossing was worth preserving as it was the last surviving example of a swing-span bridge in New Zealand and was recognised by both Heritage New Zealand and Engineering New Zealand for its heritage value. After more than six years of negotiations with the New Zealand Transport Agency, the Trust took over management of the bridge in March 2018. The agreement gave the Trust five years to manage the bridge, with the option of handing it back if it could no longer maintain the structure.How the historic bridge is being restored for walkers and cyclistsThe plan of the Trust is to restore the structure as a pedestrian and cycleway alongside the Hauraki Rail Trail. The bridge could also become a useful place for fishing. A wider cycleway through the Thames district could eventually connect it with other parts of the area. Restoration work has already taken place. Electrical work and conservation planning have been completed, while gates, bollards and safety signs have also been installed. The pilot house on the centre span was restored and repainted in its heritage colours in 2025. Railing restoration was completed in 2026, although more railing work and painting are yet to be completed.A historic crossing prepared for a new chapterThe restoration is intended to keep the Kopu Bridge connected to the community while protecting its historic character. The Trust says restoring it for public use will cost far less than the demolition estimate made years ago. It also expects the project to bring recreational, tourism and economic benefits to Kopu, Thames and the wider Coromandel Peninsula. The bridge has already had several different roles, as it was built to support road travel and accommodate river traffic, later became associated with summer traffic queues, and was eventually replaced by the new crossing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: NTA: India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
articles.summary: As exam scandals persist, critics ask whether fixing the centralised testing agency is enough or if the model needs to change.
articles.body:
In 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations.

Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations.

Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research.

But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own.

In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister.

In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system.

For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu.

A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which have reportedly been fully implemented.

The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses.

Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink.

BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible.

"Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC.

"We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres."

But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says.

Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government.

"When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains.

Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed.

Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages.

Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says.

"Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains.

Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places.

India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University.

"This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says.

For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation.

Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak.

"It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said.

The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures.

"The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again."

Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs.

The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects.

Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September.

"I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?"

Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether.

Educationists argue that scrapping the agency would not solve the underlying problem.

The NTA needs deep structural reform to address recurring failures, but abolishing it is not the answer, said M Jagadesh Kumar, former chairman of India's universities regulator.

"A single national testing body offers common security standards, technology, candidate services and result procedures. Creating many new agencies could duplicate costs and produce uneven safeguards," he told PTI news agency.

"It is not a case of all bad news. The body has conducted several exams successfully, where we did not hear of any leaks," he said.

What is needed, he argues, is a statutory institution staffed by specialists with the academic, technical and operational expertise to run a secure examination system.

Yet for some experts, the debate ultimately goes beyond the NTA itself.

Aiyar says the bigger issue is not just stopping the next paper leak, but whether a highly centralised testing system can cope with the intense competition for limited educational opportunities.

The NTA may be able to make exams more secure, she says. "But it cannot, at least on its own, change a system in which millions of students compete for a limited number of seats and a single exam can shape their future."

Some experts say reform must go beyond the NTA itself: India needs an exam system less reliant on one-off, high-stakes tests, gives students multiple chances and can better withstand disruptions.

Rao remains optimistic that the task force led by Nilekani will help plug gaps in the existing system.

But for many students, another committee offers little reassurance unless it produces changes they can actually see.

"I am studying for my university entrance examination next year," said a 16-year-old Grade 12 student.

"In my head I am prepared that there might be a leak. But what can we do about it? I will prepare and hope for the best."

articles.title: Indonesia fires: The volunteer firefighters risking their lives to defuse 'carbon bombs'
articles.summary: Peat fires in Borneo are releasing ancient stores of carbon - and sending a toxic smog across South East Asia.
articles.body:
The sky grows heavy in Borneo, though not with rain. The air, amber-hued and treacle-thick, is smudged under a blanket of smog that has spilled across international borders – to Singapore, Manila, Kuala Lumpur.

Down on the ground, smoke steams from the soil.

"It hits your nose straight away, your eyes burn – that's more or less what it's like," he says. "People say these fires are extraordinary because of the flames and the smoke. And they're right."

The 35-year-old volunteer firefighter has spent more than a month enveloped in this haze, breathing toxic millennia-old microparticles of carbon as he toils against a seemingly inextinguishable fire front.

Using hand tools, carts and portable fire pumps, he and thousands of other volunteer firefighters – many of them indigenous Dayak or Banjar people – are up against an inferno that has carbonised some 200,000 hectares of forest and farmland across Indonesian Borneo since early July.

Underground and out of sight, giant subterranean peat fires continue to smoulder, choking the air with poisonous fumes.

"Once a fire becomes uncontrolled, it harms many people. Not just humans, but also animals and plants," Sujatmoko says. "If underground fire spreads and can no longer be controlled, the losses are enormous."

Indonesia is in the throes of a wildfire catastrophe.

Amid a so-called "Super El Niño" that has supercharged local drought conditions, thousands of active fire hotspots are spreading and multiplying across the country, fuelling a transnational haze crisis that is the region's worst in more than a decade.

But what makes Borneo's fires particularly worrying is the fact that they are burning through one of the world's largest tropical peatland ecosystems.

This 4.5-million-hectare swathe of forest and swamp, under normal conditions, serves as a valuable reservoir for ancient carbon.

When these peatlands catch fire, they risk releasing millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane into the atmosphere – a "pulse" of greenhouse gas emissions that has earned them the sobriquet of "carbon bomb".

"Peatlands are incredibly effective carbon stores because their waterlogged conditions slow decomposition, allowing carbon to accumulate underground for thousands of years," explains Dr Nisa Novita, a peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN).

"But this also means they can become a 'carbon bomb' when they are drained or burned, because that carbon can be rapidly released into the atmosphere.

"Tropical peatlands in Indonesia are among the world's most effective natural carbon stores. The deeper the peat, the greater the carbon stock – and in Kalimantan, we have found peat deposits that can exceed 20 metres in depth."

A peatland that deep has been known to harbour more than 6,000 tonnes of carbon – roughly equivalent to the annual CO₂ emissions of 4,800 cars – per hectare. And when it burns, says Dr Nisa, that fossilised carbon can be released into the atmosphere "very rapidly".

Thousands of people across South East Asia are now feeling the effects of those emissions in their eyes, chests and throats.

Across Indonesia as well as Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, air pollution indices have soared to "unhealthy" extremes - almost 75 times the World Health Organization's recommended level, in some cases – and hospital admissions have surged.

Between July and August, Indonesia's Health Ministry recorded over 50,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to land and forest fires. More than 12,000 of them were children under the age of five.

"Everybody who's living within that pollution cloud is breathing in the products of those smouldering peat fires," says Susan Page, a professor at the University of Leicester's school of geology and the environment, who's been researching peatlands in Asia for three decades.

"They're breathing in carbon monoxide, which is toxic, and they're breathing in the very finely divided particulate matter... [which] can pass through the alveoli in the lungs into the bloodstream and cause further problems elsewhere in the body, including issues with the heart.

"Living in this kind of pollution cloud is extremely unhealthy."

Nowhere are these health impacts being felt more acutely than at the coalface of the disaster: the fire front.

Here, volunteer firefighters have been risking their lives and lungs to extinguish burning peatlands which are notoriously difficult to put out. Two volunteers in Central Kalimantan have died in recent days, reportedly after their health deteriorated from putting out fires.

Cloaked in toxic haze that can burn years off a person's lifespan, volunteers have been digging ponds, canals and borewells through bone-dry peat in a desperate attempt to keep their hoses tapped.

Some have been driving pipes into the earth, making ad hoc irrigation systems to combat subterranean fires. Others have been sleeping within a stone's throw of the frontline so they can battle the blazes through the night.

"The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin Ramadhianto, a volunteer firefighter in South Kalimantan's Banjarbaru, one of the worst-hit areas.

"The smell is like decaying wood being burned – that's the characteristic smell of peat. And that peat contains decomposed wood and organic material from many different sources."

Indonesia's peatland fires are not a new phenomenon.

Experts say the crisis is rooted in decades of land-use change, dating back to the Suharto era, when vast areas of rainforest and peatland in Kalimantan were opened for logging, plantations and large-scale development projects.

Yet authorities have historically avoided blaming industrial actors for causing large-scale fires.

Instead, the same indigenous communities who are now engaged in firefighting operations across the island have often been accused of triggering the blazes, due to traditional farming methods that use controlled burns to clear away vegetation.

Tono, a representative of the Dayak Kanayatn people of West Kalimantan, told the BBC that Dayak communities are frequently used as scapegoats, despite carrying out land clearing with extensive planning, caution and adherence to multi-generational customs.

Tono says these communities' traditional practices, known as uma bukit or "hill farming", are rooted in the idea of maintaining balance with nature.

But the natural balance is fast unravelling in Kalimantan, the most deforested area in Indonesia.

The region lost almost 160,000 hectares of forest area in 2025, more than one-third of the nationwide figure – much of it to make way for plantations and monocrop agriculture.

It is these same industrial-scale development projects that have been largely responsible for draining the area's peat swamps, which renders them significantly more fire-prone, Prof Page says.

"Peatlands aren't really the ideal place to set up a plantation – but of course, once the more suitable mineral soils had been exhausted it became possible, by using large machinery, to drain the peatlands and create conditions which would be dry enough," she says.

"So not only have you got the deforestation, but peatland drainage of course has also greatly increased the fire risk."

Page also points out that, whether on fire or not, a drained peatland emits carbon dioxide into the atmosphere "all of the time".

"I think that's forgotten," she says. "I think it's important to recognise that when we see the fires, they're like a dramatic example of what is actually going on the whole time in a drained peatland... The fires are just the worst expression of [that]."

Now, as these latest fires continue to spiral out of control, Sujatmoko and others face a concatenation of difficulties in the coming days, weeks and months – not least of which is a shortage of water.

Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge", Sujatmoko explains.

Even then there is a high chance the fire will reappear, like a smoking revenant, fed by hidden fuel buried in the invisible depths of the peat swamp.

In the face of these persistent reignitions, ongoing drought conditions and toxic smog, fatigue is another concern.

"We're definitely tired," says Sujatmoko.

"We get exhausted, we miss our families, our children, our wives. But for now, all of us are putting those things aside. We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty."

"We also hope rain comes soon," he adds. "We've spent months away from home... May all the efforts of those on the front lines be a blessing for everyone."

Additional reporting by Faisal Irfani from BBC Indonesian.

articles.title: The £70 refund letter that isn't a scam
articles.summary: About one million people - mostly women - are owed pension tax relief and will be contacted by HMRC.
articles.body:
You may be among the one million people, mostly women, who will receive letters explaining how you are eligible for top-up pension payments - and it's not a scam.

Those entitled are low earners who have missed out on the money because of the way their pension is administered.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) will write to people over the next few months, explaining how to receive the payment. Typically they will be due £70, but that may vary considerably depending on their circumstances.

Anyone eligible will be contacted automatically but, if you receive a letter, there are various checks you can do to ensure the letter is genuine so you don't get hoodwinked.

When you pay into a pension, the government allows some of the money that would otherwise have been paid in tax to go towards your pension instead. This is known as tax relief .

For relatively complicated reasons, some low earners whose employer used what's known as a Net Pay Arrangement pension scheme received less than those whose pension was administered through a Relief at Source scheme.

Employees have no control over the type of scheme that's used, so the government has decided to top up those who have missed out, through what's called a low earner's pension payment.

Typically, they would have earned close to, but not more than, £12,570 a year (the starting point for paying income tax).

Top-up payments will initially be paid for the 2024-25 tax year, with automated payments subsequently kicking in for later years.

Customers don't need to apply. If eligible, you'll be sent information by HMRC - the UK's tax authority - in a letter or through your online personal tax account .

HMRC will not text, email or call you about it. If you receive such a call or message, it is a scam. Also, it will never ask you to transfer money, or ask for PIN codes or passwords.

Other ways to check contact is smooth and genuine include:

Making sure HMRC has your latest address

Searching Gov.uk for "check if a letter you've received from HMRC is genuine", and look for "Low Earner's Pension Payment"

Customers will be asked to provide their bank details through their personal tax account. Customers who are digitally excluded will be able to phone HMRC to accept their payment instead

"We know some people may be cautious about unexpected contact, which is why we provide clear information about what to expect and how to verify the contact is genuine," said a HMRC spokesman.

"Customers can check a letter is genuine on Gov.uk and should only respond via official HMRC channels."

Sir Steve Webb, partner at pensions consultancy LCP and a former pensions minister, said he was shocked at how few people the government expected to actually receive the payment.

The government has estimated the cost of the project to be much lower than if everyone who was eligible took up the payment.

"The process of getting these payments to the right people is going to be incredibly painful and there is a real risk of huge non take-up," he said.

"It is vital that communications are effective to make sure that people get the money to which they are entitled."

HMRC says it will run an awareness campaign using social media and other channels.

You could be missing out on £150 off your energy bill - here's how to check

It may be easier to get your first mortgage than you think - here's why
